name: APT19
affiliation_detail: FireEye assessed it as "composed of freelancers, with some degree of sponsorship by the Chinese government."
description:
APT19 (also known as Codoso Team, C0d0so0, and Sunshop Group) is a Chinese cyber espionage group active since at least 2010. 
The group has targeted a wide range of sectors including defense, finance, energy, pharmaceutical, telecommunications, high-tech, education, manufacturing, legal services, government, think tanks, and political dissidents. 
APT19 is best known for two high-profile campaigns: the 2014 Forbes.com watering hole attack, in which the group chained two zero-day exploits (Adobe Flash CVE-2014-9163 and an IE ASLR bypass) to compromise visitors from U.S. defense and financial firms; and a 2017 phishing campaign targeting seven global law and investment firms using CVE-2017-0199, macro-enabled Excel documents, and Cobalt Strike. 
The group's earliest known operation was the 2010 compromise of the Norwegian Nobel Peace Prize Committee website using a Firefox zero-day, likely motivated by the award to Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo. 
APT19 relies heavily on Derusbi, a malware family assessed as unique to Chinese espionage operators. The group is connected to the "Sunshop Digital Quartermaster" — a suspected common malware development entity that FireEye assessed supports as many as 11 separate APT campaigns. APT19's relationship to Deep Panda (G0009) is actively debated: Malpedia and some sources treat them as the same entity, while MITRE and iSIGHT maintain them as separate (but possibly related) groups sharing tools like Derusbi.
Aliases Notes:
The aliases and overlapping groups landscape around APT19 remains rather tangled. The core question: Are APT19, Deep Panda, Shell Crew, Black Vine, and related designations the same group, overlapping groups, or a broader ecosystem?
MITRE maintains separate entries: APT19 (G0073) and Deep Panda (G0009). MITRE explicitly states: "Some analysts track APT19 and Deep Panda as the same group, but it is unclear from open source information if the groups are the same." The G0073 entry references FireEye (2017 law firm phishing), Palo Alto (C0d0so0 attacks), and iSIGHT/Dark Reading (Forbes watering hole). The G0009 entry references CrowdStrike (think tank targeting), RSA (Shell Crew), ThreatConnect (Anthem breach), and Symantec (Black Vine).
iSIGHT Partners (2015) explicitly stated that while Codoso Team "shares attack techniques with Deep Panda, which like Codoso, leans heavily on the use of the Derusbi malware," iSIGHT "believes them to be two distinct gangs." The shared use of Derusbi may reflect the Sunshop Digital Quartermaster — a suspected common malware supplier — rather than organizational identity.
Malpedia merges all these aliases under a single APT19 entry (including Deep Panda, Shell Crew, Black Vine, KungFu Kittens, etc.). The CFR Cyber Operations Tracker similarly lists them together.
* The most recent APT19-specific public reporting is FireEye's June 2017 law firm phishing campaign. If Deep Panda is considered the same group, Fortinet reported Deep Panda exploiting VMware Horizon servers in 2022.

campaigns.name: Nobel Peace Prize Committee Website Compromise
campaigns.description: APT19/Sunshop Group compromised the website of the Norwegian Nobel Peace Prize Committee shortly after the 2010 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Liu Xiaobo, a Chinese dissident. The attack leveraged a zero-day vulnerability in Mozilla Firefox to serve exploits to visitors via a watering hole. iSIGHT's John Hultquist noted the connection between the award to a Chinese dissident and the immediate compromise of the committee's website. FireEye later linked this attack to the Sunshop Group based on shared TTPs including zero-day exploitation and strategic web compromise.

campaigns.name: Sunshop Campaign (IE/Java Zero-Day)
campaigns.description: FireEye identified a campaign exploiting the IE zero-day CVE-2013-1347 (affecting IE 8) and Java exploits CVE-2013-2423 and CVE-2013-1493. Attackers compromised multiple legitimate websites and inserted malicious JavaScript redirecting visitors to an exploit server at sunshop[.]com[.]tw (the infrastructure that gave the group its name). Successful exploitation delivered Poison Ivy RAT and Briba backdoor. A related U.S. Department of Labor watering hole (noted by CrowdStrike and AlienVault) targeted pages with nuclear-related content — likely aimed at Department of Energy employees.

campaigns.name: NGO/Non-Profit Targeting Campaign
campaigns.description: FireEye uncovered a campaign targeting non-profit organizations and non-governmental organizations by compromising legitimate websites. Attackers inserted iframes into legitimate sites to redirect visitors to attacker-controlled IP addresses serving Poison Ivy RAT. FireEye identified the involvement of the Sunshop Digital Quartermaster through a shared RT_MANIFEST resource ("Sunshop Manifest") previously observed in 86 other samples.

campaigns.name: Forbes.com Watering Hole Attack
campaigns.description: APT19/Codoso Team compromised the Forbes.com "Thought of the Day" Flash widget, which appeared to every visitor on the site (ranked 61st most popular in the US by Alexa). The attack chained two zero-day exploits: an Adobe Flash vulnerability (CVE-2014-9163, patched December 9, 2014) and a previously unknown Internet Explorer ASLR bypass allowing execution of the Flash exploit. Invincea described the chained zero-day technique as "a unicorn" in sophistication, comparing it to Stuxnet. Despite the massive reach of Forbes.com, the attack narrowly targeted visitors from U.S. defense contractors and financial services firms. Additional websites were found targeting Chinese dissident groups with the same exploit, deployed before its public disclosure. Derusbi malware variants were delivered as payloads. iSIGHT attributed the attack to Codoso Team based on simplified Chinese code, Derusbi (unique to Chinese operators), and C2 domain connections to previous Codoso campaigns. Invincea first detected the attack through a defense industry customer.

campaigns.name: C0d0so0 Multi-Industry Campaign
campaigns.description: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 identified a new wave of attacks by C0d0so0 targeting organizations in the telecommunications, high-tech, education, manufacturing, and legal services sectors. Two malware variants were deployed: an HTTP-based variant disguised as an AVG AntiVirus serial number generator, and a newer variant using a custom network protocol over port 22 disguised as a DLL side-loaded by a legitimate McAfee application. Both variants shared network communication structure similar to Derusbi, with campaign-specific compile times only days before observed attacks. C2 domains were registered with Chinese addresses and resolved to a Hong Kong IP. Notably, several targeted hosts were server systems rather than user endpoints, suggesting APT19 was building infrastructure for future watering hole attacks. Unit 42 established code lineage to the Forbes.com attack through shared single-byte XOR encryption routines and overlapping strings.

campaigns.name: Law and Investment Firm Phishing Campaign
campaigns.description: FireEye observed a phishing campaign targeting at least seven global law and investment firms. APT19 used three different techniques across the campaign, showing rapid adaptation. FireEye stated they had "previously observed APT19 steal data from law and investment firms for competitive economic purposes." FireEye had not observed post-exploitation activity at time of publication.
